summary: Cast-iron and brick light on the Nubble off York Beach, Maine. Lit 1879 with a fourth-order lens; automated 1987; owned by the Town of York.

structures.note: Cast-iron tower lined with brick, 41 ft to the center of the lantern (archive; LighthouseFriends). The nomination gives 39 ft.
Story-and-a-half wood-frame keeper's house of six rooms, joined to the tower by a covered way (nomination). Victorian style (archive).
Boathouse and boat slip built 1888 (LighthouseFriends). The archive lists a boathouse built 1978.

access.note: Grounds open; dwelling and tower closed (LighthouseFriends). The archive lists the station as open to the public. Most visitors view it from Sohier Park on the mainland.

facts.agency: Town of York (owner); U.S. Coast Guard (owner at the 1985 nomination)

events.note: Local mariners asked for a light on the Nubble (LighthouseFriends).
Congress appropriated $5,000 for a light on 3 March 1837; Captain Joseph Smith advised against it and proposed a beacon on York Ledge (LighthouseFriends).
Bark Isidore wrecked north of the Nubble, near Bald Head Cliff, in November 1842 (LighthouseFriends only).
Congress appropriated $5,000 for a light on the Nubble or at York Harbor; the money was withdrawn after a coast survey (LighthouseFriends).
Lighthouse Board requested $15,000 for construction (LighthouseFriends).
Cast-iron tower erected; sections made in Portland, shipped on the USS Myrtle in April 1879.
Fourth-order red light first exhibited 1 July 1879 (LighthouseFriends).
Fourth-order Fresnel (archive record).
Boathouse and boat slip built (LighthouseFriends).
Striking machine moved from Pond Island and set up; bell changed to an outside striker (LighthouseFriends).
Fog bell disabled 16 April, repaired 20 April 1896.
Telephone connection to the village of York Beach (LighthouseFriends).
Tower painted white again, 1 September 1899 (Board report; LighthouseFriends).
Boat slip extended about 40 feet; about 50 boulders removed; storm porch built at the tower.
Red brick oil house added (archive; LighthouseFriends).
Frame bell tower replaced by an enclosed pyramidal tower, which stayed until 1961 (LighthouseFriends).
Burke towed a disabled launch to the station in a heavy southwesterly wind and kept her occupants overnight (12 September 1913).
Burke saved a man from probable drowning (13 June 1914).
Richardson assisted two men drifting to sea in a rowboat (10 October 1920).
Richardson towed a disabled sloop to anchorage and piloted her to York Harbor; date within fiscal 1921 not given.
Explosion damaged the fourth-order lens; a duplicate was brought from another station (LighthouseFriends).
Moore helped tow a speed boat and its occupant to the station (10 July 1928).
Station electrified; kerosene vapor lamp retired (LighthouseFriends).
Pyramidal bell tower removed (LighthouseFriends).
Nomination prepared January 1985 by the Maine Historic Preservation Commission; listing date not read in the sources.
Automated (archive; LighthouseFriends).
Town adopted the station under the Maine Lights Program (LighthouseFriends).
Blizzard on 26 December arced the power lines; the beacon ran on battery and went out two days later (LighthouseFriends).
Winter storm destroyed the overhead tram used to bring supplies, and damaged its shed (LighthouseFriends).
Coast Guard installed a solar light on 16 April 2013 (LighthouseFriends).
Repainting and replacement of the overhead zipline (LighthouseFriends).
$42,000 project to replace the back deck and tower windows (LighthouseFriends).

Disabled in a heavy southwesterly wind; towed to the light station, occupants kept overnight (keeper Burke).

notes_for_editor: (1) Simon Leighton: the archive lists him for 1879; LighthouseFriends says an illness kept him from taking the post, and calls Otterson the first keeper. Unresolved. (2) Eugene L. Coleman's end year: archive 1942, LighthouseFriends 1946. The archive date is used. (3) Tower height: nomination 39 ft; archive and LighthouseFriends 41 ft to the lantern center. The story uses 41 ft. (4) Characteristic: the record's 'Iso R 6s' is not confirmed by any source read here. LighthouseFriends gives a fourth-order fixed red light in 1879; Wikipedia (lead only) gives 'Isophase Red 5s'. The characteristic is omitted from the facts until checked against the Coast Guard Light List. (5) The record's range (13 nm) is not in any source read; omitted. (6) The 1842 Isidore wreck, the 1807 request, the 1837 and 1852 appropriations, the 1874 request, the 1890 striking machine, the 1898 telephone, the 1928 lens explosion, the 1967 basket photograph and the 1986-87 family supply are all from LighthouseFriends alone. The 1842 wreck is not confirmed elsewhere. (7) Fiscal 1921 and 1920: the Bulletin's 10 October 1920 rowboat rescue and the Commissioner's fiscal 1921 rowboat rescue may be one event; the story says so. The Vava rescue is undated within fiscal 1921. (8) OCR of the 1913 Bulletin is poor; the evidence quote is the name and date only. The rest of that item is paraphrased from the same page. (9) The Chronicling America searches for Cape Neddick failed with HTTP 520 from loc.gov. No newspaper source is used. (10) The 1967 child is not named (private person). The keeper David K. Winchester's name is in the roster, as the archive prints it. (11) Wikipedia (lead only) gives an NRHP date of 16 April 1985, not confirmed by a source read; no date is entered. (12) Keeper names after 1960 appear only in the roster as the archive prints them. (13) Fact-check 2026-10-22: the nomination gives the tower as 39 ft (NRHP 'The 39 foot light tower'); the archive and LighthouseFriends give 41 ft to the center of the lantern. The story states both. (14) The 1928 Bulletin prints the keeper who towed the speed boat as 'F. C. Moore' (and the 1924-1929 index as 'Moore, F.C.'); the 1923 Bulletin names 'Fairfield H. Moore' as keeper of Cape Neddick for the same period. The story says only 'Moore' for 1928 and does not state the initials. The identification rests on the surname, the station and the archive's 1921-1928 tenure. (15) The 1913 Bulletin (PDF p.42) is badly OCR'd: the evidence quotes are the exact OCR fragments for the name, date and the 'heavy southwesterly wind' phrase; the rest of the sentence ('took care of its occupants overnight') is a faithful reading of the same OCR line. (16) The 1921 Commissioner entry (scan p.663) describes Richardson's rowboat rescue of two men without a date; the story says it may be the same event as the 10 October 1920 Bulletin entry (scan p.44 of the 1920 Bulletin), and does not assert it. (17) The Portsmouth Journal notice on ten-cent ferrying and the 1837 Captain Smith letter are known only as LighthouseFriends quotes them; the story attributes them to LighthouseFriends. (18) The 1967 child, the 1986-87 keeper's family, and the post-1960 keepers are not named in the story; the roster lists them as the archive prints them.
